h: Judah Offers Himself for the Community

p: וַיִּגַּשׁ אֵלָיו יְהוּדָה וְגוֹמֵר.
— “Judah approached him,” and so forth.

לְהָבִין עִנְיַן הַגָּשָׁה זוֹ אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר אָמַר יְהוּדָה מַה נֹּאמַר לַאֲדוֹנִי וְגוֹמֵר שֶׁהִצְדִּיק הַדִּין עַל נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁכּוּלָּם יִהְיוּ עֲבָדִים וְאַחַר זֶה כַּאֲשֶׁר הֵנִיחַ לָהֶם יוֹסֵף שֶׁרַק מִי שֶׁנִּמְצָא בְיָדוֹ יִהְיֶה עֶבֶד נִגַּשׁ בְּתוֹכָחוֹת גַּם עַל זֶה.

— We must understand this approach. Judah had already said, “What can we say to my lord?” and so forth, accepting the justice of all of them becoming slaves. Yet after Joseph released them, saying that only the one in whose possession the goblet was found would be a slave, Judah approached to protest even this.

וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר בָּזֶה דְּהִנֵּה כַּאֲשֶׁר נִמְצָא הַגָּבִיעַ בְּיָדָם וְהָיָה הַמִּשְׁפָּט עַל פִּי דִינֵיהֶם שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כּוּלָּם עֲבָדִים וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעַצְמָם אֲשֶׁר יִמָּצֵא וְגוֹמֵר וְגַם אֲנַחְנוּ נִהְיֶה לַאֲדוֹנִי לַעֲבָדִים,

— We may explain that when the goblet was found among them, their own law required them all to become slaves. They themselves had said, “The one with whom it is found,” and so forth, “and we too will become slaves to my lord.”

אָזַי הִרְגִּישׁ יְהוּדָה בְּעַצְמוֹ אֲשֶׁר הַמִּשְׁפָּט צֶדֶק בָּא עֲלֵיהֶם מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם לְשַׁלֵּם לָהֶם כְּפִי מִדָּתָם שֶׁמָּכְרוּ אֶת יוֹסֵף לְעֶבֶד וַעֲבוּר זֶה הִצְדִּיק עַל נַפְשָׁם שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כֻּלָּם עֲבָדִים,
— Judah then sensed that this just judgment came upon them from Heaven, measure for measure, for selling Joseph as a slave. He therefore accepted their all becoming slaves as just.
גַּם בִּנְיָמִין הֲגַם שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בִּמְכִירָתוֹ כִּי הָעוֹלָם נִידּוֹן אַחַר רוּבּוֹ וּכְמוֹ רְאוּבֵן שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה גַּם כֵּן בִּמְכִירָתוֹ.
— This included Benjamin, although he had not participated in the sale, because the world is judged according to its majority—just as Reuven too had not participated in the sale.
וְהָיָה סָבוּר שֶׁהוּא מִשְׁפָּט מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר הָאֱלֹהִים מָצָא וְגוֹמֵר,
— He believed this was Hashem’s judgment, as he said, “God has discovered,” and so forth.

p: אָמְנָם כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר לָהֶם יוֹסֵף שֶׁרַק בִּנְיָמִין יִהְיֶה עֶבֶד אָזַי נִתְיַישֵּׁב יְהוּדָה בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁזֶּה לֹא בָּא מִצַּד עוֹנֶשׁ שֶׁל הַמְּכִירָה.
— But when Joseph said that only Benjamin would become a slave, Judah concluded that this was not punishment for the sale.

רַק שֶׁזֶּה בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁנִּמְכַּר יוֹסֵף לְעֶבֶד מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם נְסִבָּה כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּתְקַיֵּים עַל יָדוֹ גְּזֵרַת בֵּין הַבְּתָרִים וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִינּוּ אוֹתָם וְדַיְיקָא עַל יְדֵי יוֹסֵף מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהוּא הָיָה הַמּוּבְחָר שֶׁבָּהֶם.

— Rather, Joseph’s being sold as a slave had itself been arranged from Heaven to fulfill through him the decree of the Covenant between the Pieces, “They will enslave and afflict them”—specifically through Joseph, because he was the choicest among them.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁרָאוּ שֶׁהִתְאַבֵּל יַעֲקֹב עָלָיו יָמִים רַבִּים שֶׁמִּזֶּה הוֹכִיחוּ שֶׁיּוֹסֵף הָיָה צַדִּיק בֶּאֱמֶת.
— They had seen Jacob mourn him for many days, from which they inferred that Joseph was truly righteous.
וְסָבַר שֶׁלָּזֶה נִבְחַר הוּא לְהַשְׁלִים בּוֹ הָעִינּוּי.
— Judah therefore believed that Joseph had been chosen to complete the allotted affliction.

שֶׁכְּבָר אָמַרְנוּ שֶׁיַּעֲקֹב הָיָה סָבוּר שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְקַיֵּים עַל יָדוֹ הָעַבְדוּת וְהָעִינּוּי שֶׁסָּבַל אֵצֶל לָבָן וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר הָיִיתִי בַיּוֹם אֲכָלַנִי חוֹרֶב וְגוֹמֵר וְעַל כֵּן בִּיקֵּשׁ יַעֲקֹב לֵישֵׁב בְּשַׁלְוָה (וְנִתְבָּאֵר וַיֵּשֶׁב מַאֲמָר א׳),

— We have explained that Jacob thought he had already fulfilled the enslavement and affliction through his suffering with Lavan: “By day the scorching heat consumed me,” and so forth. Jacob therefore wished to dwell in tranquility (as explained in Vayeshev, discourse 1).
וְהָיָה יְהוּדָה סָבוּר שֶׁנִּבְחַר יוֹסֵף לְהַשְׁלִים עַל יָדוֹ הָעַבְדוּת וְהָעִינּוּי.
— Judah thought that Joseph had been chosen to complete the enslavement and affliction.

וְהִנֵּה עַתָּה כַּאֲשֶׁר רוֹצֶה מוֹשֵׁל מִצְרַיִם שֶׁבִּנְיָמִין יִהְיֶה עֶבֶד דָּן יְהוּדָה מִזֶּה שֶׁבְּוַדַּאי יוֹסֵף מֵת כְּבָר וְעַל כֵּן נִבְחַר בִּנְיָמִין מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם לְקִיּוּם גְּזֵרַת הָעַבְדוּת תַּחְתָּיו.

— Now that Egypt’s ruler wanted Benjamin as a slave, Judah inferred that Joseph must already have died, and Benjamin had therefore been chosen from Heaven to fulfill the decree of enslavement in his place.
וּבָזֶה יוּנַח מַה שֶּׁאָמַר כָּאן וְאָחִיו מֵת וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר אָמְרוּ וְהָאֶחָד אֵינֶנּוּ,
— This explains his saying here, “His brother is dead,” although they had previously said, “One is no longer here.”

וַהֲגַם שֶׁפֵּרֵשׁ רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי שֶׁמִּפְּנֵי הַיִּרְאָה אָמְרוּ וְכוּלֵי כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמַר הֲבִיאֻהוּ אֶצְלִי אֵינוֹ מוּבָן שֶׁכְּבָר אָמְרוּ וְהָאֶחָד אֵינֶנּוּ וּמַה יּוֹעִיל אִם לֹא יִרְצֶה לְהַאֲמִינָם מַה שֶּׁאוֹמְרִים שֶׁמֵּת.

— Although Rashi explains that they said it out of fear, and so forth, lest he demand, “Bring him to me,” this is difficult: they had already said “One is no longer here.” How would saying he was dead help if the ruler refused to believe them?
גַּם מֵהֵיכָן יְבִיאוּהוּ כֵּיוָן שֶׁאָמְרוּ שֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ וְלֹא יָדְעוּ מְקוֹמוֹ.
— And where could they bring him from, when they had said he was gone and did not know his whereabouts?
וּלְפִי דְבָרֵינוּ אָמַר זֶה לִדְבַר אֱמֶת כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁדָּן בְּדַעְתּוֹ שֶׁכְּבָר מֵת.
— According to our explanation, Judah spoke truthfully, in accordance with his own inference that Joseph had already died.

p: וְעַל זֶה הִתְחִיל עַתָּה לְהִתְמַרְמֵר מְאֹד בְּנַפְשׁוֹ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁגַּם עַל יוֹסֵף הָיָה הוּא עִיקַּר הַגּוֹרֵם לְצַעֵר אֶת אָבִיו בַּאֲבֵילוּת וְעַתָּה נוֹסַף עוֹד שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָעַרְבוּת שֶׁלּוֹ יִגְרוֹם חָלִילָה מִיתָה לְאָבִיו,

— This filled him with deep bitterness: he had been chiefly responsible for causing his father to mourn Joseph, and now, through his guarantee for Benjamin, he would bring about his father’s death, Heaven forbid.
וְעַל כֵּן נִגַּשׁ בִּמְרִירוּת נַפְשׁוֹ לְבַקֵּשׁ בִּתְפִלָּה שֶׁיִּתְקַבֵּל הוּא לְעֶבֶד וְיִתְקַיֵּים בּוֹ הָעַבְדוּת וְהָעִינּוּי וְהַנַּעַר יַעַל עִם אֶחָיו.
— He therefore approached in anguish, praying that he be accepted as a slave, fulfilling the enslavement and affliction himself, while the boy returned with his brothers.
כִּי כָּל דִּבְרֵי יְהוּדָה הָיָה נִשְׁמָעִים לְכָאן וּלְכָאן שֶׁבִּפְשׁוּטוֹ דִיבֵּר לְיוֹסֵף וְהַדְּבָרִים הַלָּלוּ בְּעַצְמָם הָיָה כַוָּנָתוֹ לִתְפִלָּה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
— All Judah’s words carried a dual meaning. On the plain level he addressed Joseph, while through those very words he intended a prayer to Hashem.
בִּי אֲדֹנִי יְדַבֶּר נָא עַבְדְּךָ דָבָר בְּאָזְנֵי אֲדֹנִי וְגוֹמֵר הַכֹּל הַמְכוּוָּן לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
— “Please, my lord, let your servant speak a word in my lord’s ears,” and so forth—all was directed toward Hashem.
אֲדֹנִי שָׁאַל וְגוֹמֵר שֶׁיָּדַע שֶׁכָּל הַמְּאוֹרָע מֵהַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מַה שֶּׁשָּׁאַל אוֹתָם וּמַה שֶּׁצִּוָּה שֶׁיָּבִיאוּ אֶת בִּנְיָמִין.
— “My lord asked,” and so forth: he knew that everything that had happened was under His providence—the ruler’s questioning them and ordering them to bring Benjamin.

וּכְעֵין מַה שֶּׁפֵּרֵשׁ הָרַב מְנַחֵם עֲזַרְיָה גַּבֵּי נְחֶמְיָה דִּכְתִיב וָאֶתְפַּלֵּל אֶל אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וָאוֹמַר לַמֶּלֶךְ וְגוֹמֵר שֶׁאַף שֶׁלֹּא מָצִינוּ שָׁם שׁוּם תְּפִלָּה רַק הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁדִּיבֵּר לַמֶּלֶךְ הָיָה כַוָּנָתוֹ בִּתְפִלָּה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.

— This resembles Rabbi Menachem Azariah’s explanation concerning Nechemiah: “I prayed to the God of Heaven, and said to the king,” and so forth. Although no prayer is explicitly recorded there, the words he addressed to the king were intended as a prayer to Hashem.
וְכֵן בְּכָאן הָיוּ דִבְרֵי יְהוּדָה שֶׁאָמַר לְיוֹסֵף בִּמְכוּוָּן לְהִתְפַּלֵּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
— Here too, Judah’s words to Joseph were intended as a prayer to Hashem.

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה שֶׁנִּגַּשׁ לְמִלְחָמָה וּלְפִיּוּס וּלְתְפִלָּה עַיֵּן שָׁם אַף שֶׁלֹּא מָצִינוּ כָּאן שׁוּם תְּפִלָּה רַק הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁדִּיבֵּר לְיוֹסֵף הָיוּ דִּבְרֵי תְפִלָּה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
— Hence Bereishit Rabbah teaches that he approached for battle, conciliation, and prayer; see there. Although no prayer appears here explicitly, his words to Joseph were words of prayer to Hashem.

In the preceding portion he had said, ‘Here we are, slaves to my lord.’ It seemed that he had begun to despair, and he regarded his undertaking to his father concerning Benjamin in both worlds as a mistake. In this portion he greatly strengthened himself before God: although I acted improperly, nevertheless God has the power to save me. This is ‘Judah approached him’—‘him’ means the depths of Joseph’s heart, until Joseph was compelled to reveal himself to them. For all these verses are an argument addressed to God, while Judah thought that he stood before a gentile king and was arguing with him.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The parallel explains the inner movement that makes Judah’s speech a prayer: he turns from self-condemnation toward confidence in God’s power to help. His words can therefore address the apparent ruler while their deepest appeal reaches God—and, through that appeal, the depths of Joseph’s heart.

paragraphs.text: Rama miFano, Asarah Maamarot, Maamar Em Kol Chai I:7: “The Sages have already taught us concerning Daniel’s words when he stood before Nebuchadnezzar and said, “My lord, may the dream be for those who hate You, and its interpretation for Your enemies,” that he spoke these words toward the glory of the Shechinah. So too I say concerning Nehemiah: when Artaxerxes said to him, “Why is your face sad?” it is written, “I prayed to the God of heaven.” Could there have been time between the king’s question and Nehemiah’s answer to pray inwardly, even a short prayer? Rather, what was his prayer? The very words he spoke before the king, while his heart was directed to heaven. So too with Esther. This plainly teaches the children of Judah to take counsel within ourselves, so that Hashem is always before us and our words flow before Him in entreaty, in petition, and for all our needs.”

p: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּשֶׁהָלַךְ נֶגֶד עֵשָׂו שֶׁהִתְקִין עַצְמוֹ לְדוֹרֹן וּלְתְפִלָּה וּלְמִלְחָמָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב פֵּרוּשׁ רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי וַיִּשְׁלַח.
— Similarly, Jacob our father, peace be upon him, prepared himself for a gift, prayer, and battle when going to meet Esau, as Rashi explains in Vayishlach.

כִּי כָּל מַעֲשֵׂה אָבוֹת סִימָן לַבָּנִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב רַבִּי מֹשֶׁה בֶּן נַחְמָן וְגַם בְּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ מְרַמֵּז הַמִּדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא שֶׁכָּל עִנְיַן הִתְגַּלּוּת יוֹסֵף לְאֶחָיו הוּא מֵעֵין הִתְגַּלּוּת הַיְשׁוּעָה לֶעָתִיד.

— For every deed of the patriarchs is a sign for their descendants, as Ramban writes. In this portion too, Midrash Tanchuma indicates that Joseph’s revealing himself to his brothers prefigures the revelation of future salvation.

וְהִנֵּה כַוָּנַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּהַדּוֹרֹן יָדוּעַ שֶׁהָיָה כְּעֵין בְּחִינַת שָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים דְּאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג׳ סג א) לְמִרְמֵי לֵיהּ גַּרְמָא לְכַלְבָּא וְכוּלֵי,
— Jacob’s intention in the gift is known: it resembled the scapegoat sent away on Yom Kippur, as taught in the holy Zohar (III, 63a), “to throw a bone to the dog,” and so forth.

וּכְמוֹ כֵן הָיָה בִּיהוּדָה שֶׁכְּפִי דַעְתּוֹ הָיָה נִדּוֹן עִם מוֹשֵׁל מִצְרַיִם הִתְקִין עַצְמוֹ לְפִיּוּס שֶׁהָיָה סָבוּר שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שֶׁיַּכְנִיעַ עַצְמוֹ אֵלָיו וְקִיבֵּל עָלָיו עַבְדוּת וְיִקְרָאֵהוּ אֲדוֹנִי עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִתְפַּיֵּיס וְיִהְיֶה יוֹצֵא בָּזֶה הָעַבְדוּת.

— Similarly, Judah, believing he was contending with Egypt’s ruler, prepared for conciliation. He thought that by submitting to him, accepting slavery, and calling him “my lord,” he would appease him and thereby discharge the required enslavement.
וּבְלִבּוֹ כִּיוֵּן הַדְּבָרִים לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהָיָה תְּפִלָּה.
— In his heart, however, he directed these words to Hashem, making them a prayer.
וְהִנֵּה בְּמִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה אִיתָא מִקּוֹדֶם מַחֲלוֹקֶת רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי נְחֶמְיָה וְרַבָּנָן שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד אָמַר שֶׁהַהַגָּשָׁה הָיָה עַל אוֹפֶן אֶחָד מִשָּׁלֹשׁ הַגָּשׁוֹת הַנִּזְכָּרוֹת,
— Midrash Rabbah first records a dispute among Rabbi Judah, Rabbi Nechemyah, and the Rabbis, each interpreting the approach as one of the three approaches mentioned.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר פָּשַׁט לְהוֹן שֶׁמּוּכָן לְכָל הַשָּׁלֹשׁ דְּבָרִים לְמִלְחָמָה וּלְפִיּוּס וּלְתְפִלָּה.
— Rabbi Elazar then explained to them that Judah was prepared for all three: battle, conciliation, and prayer.

וְהַיְינוּ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָעִנְיָנִים הָאֵלּוּ מְרַמְּזִים עַל הַגְּאוּלָה הָעֲתִידָה שֶׁיּוּצְרַךְ גַּם כֵּן שָׁלֹשׁ הָעִנְיָנִים הָאֵלּוּ וְגַם בִּבְחִינָה אַחַת מֵהֶם יִהְיֶה דַּי לְפָנֵינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הִתְגַּלּוּת הַיְשׁוּעָה עַל יָדָהּ אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר סָבַלְנוּ וּכְדְאִיתָא בְּשֵׁם הַצַּדִּיקִים שֶׁעִנְיַן מִלְחֶמֶת גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג וַהֲרִיגַת מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף כְּבָר עָבַר עָלֵינוּ.

— These matters allude to the future redemption, which will also require these three elements. Yet even one of them would suffice for us to reveal salvation after all we have already suffered. Thus it is taught in the name of the righteous that the experiences of the war of Gog and Magog and the killing of Mashiach ben Joseph have already passed over us.
וּכְמוֹ כֵן יְהוּדָה הָיָה סָבוּר שֶׁכְּבָר הוּא סוֹף הַתִּיקּוּן וְנִצְרָךְ חֶבְלֵי מָשִׁיחַ וְנִסְתַּפֵּק מַה שֶּׁנִּצְרָךְ וְזֶה קִיבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ.
— Likewise, Judah thought the final rectification had arrived and the birth pangs of Mashiach were required. Unsure what was necessary, he accepted it upon himself.
וְאַחַר שֶׁקִּיבֵּל עָלָיו עַבְדוּת שֶׁיִּסְבּוֹל הוּא בְּעַד הַכְּלָל אָז וְלֹא יָכוֹל יוֹסֵף לְהִתְאַפֵּק אַף רֶגַע אֶחָד כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ עֵת הִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁלּוֹ.
— Once he accepted slavery, undertaking to suffer on behalf of the community, “Joseph could no longer restrain himself” for even a moment, for the time of his revelation had arrived.
כְּמוֹ כֵן יִהְיֶה בְּעֵת קֵץ שֶׁלֹּא יְעַכֵּב הַמָּקוֹם אַף רֶגַע וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אֲנִי הַשֵּׁם בְּעִתָּהּ אֲחִישֶׁנָּה כְּשֶׁיָּבֹא הָעֵת יִהְיֶה חִישׁ מַהֵר.
— So will it be at the appointed end: the Omnipresent will not delay even a moment. This is “I, Hashem, will hasten it in its time”: when the time arrives, it will come swiftly.

paragraphs.text: Ramban, Bereshit 12:6: “I will tell you a principle that you should understand throughout the coming passages concerning Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. It is a great matter that our Sages expressed briefly: “Everything that happened to the fathers is a sign for the children.” Therefore Scripture relates at length their journeys, the digging of wells, and their other experiences. A reader might think these details superfluous and without benefit, but they all come to teach about the future. When an event happens to a prophet from among the three patriarchs, he perceives through it what has been decreed to happen to his descendants.”

He kissed each one and wept over him, as it says, “He kissed all his brothers and wept over them.” Just as Yosef reconciled with his brothers only through weeping, so, when the Holy One, blessed be He, redeems Israel, He will redeem them through weeping: “With weeping they will come, and with supplications I will lead them. I will guide them to streams of water, on a straight path where they will not stumble, for I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is My firstborn.””

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos 2:8: “The entire sixth millennium is the preparation for the day of Shabbat, and it is the time of ‘In its time I will hasten it.’ For the plain sense is that ‘I will hasten it’ refers to ‘in its time’: even within its time there is hastening. By way of illustration, the whole day is valid for circumcision, but the zealous perform commandments early. The entire eighth day is ‘its time,’ and performing it early in the day depends on zeal. So too the entire sixth millennium is ‘in its time,’ and within it there is ‘I will hasten it’ even in its time. Had they merited, the time of ‘I will hasten it’ would have come even before ‘in its time,’ in the fifth millennium, or even right at the end of the fourth.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Here Rav Tzadok reads “I will hasten it” as applying to “in its time” itself, the reading behind his claim that when the appointed end arrives, salvation comes without a moment’s delay. The Kedushas Shabbos passage adds the comparison to the eighth day of circumcision and places this hastened time within the sixth millennium.
